source.filename: 2014-The existence of a critical length scale in regularised friction.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Linear isotropic elastic half-space under two-dimensional plane strain conditions
Rigid flat counter-surface (deformable-rigid interface)
Interface friction governed by Coulomb's law with identical static and kinetic coefficients of friction (μ = 0.75)

Regularisation governed by a simplified Prakash-Clifton friction formulation relating the rate of change of frictional strength to slip velocity, reference velocity, characteristic length scale, and normal contact stress
Absence of bulk damping (no numerical Rayleigh damping or bulk viscoelastic dissipation)
control_variables: Reference velocity V⋆ = 10^-4 m/s
Friction coefficient μ = 0.75
Remote compressive normal traction τ2^0 = 0.0150 Pa
Remote shear traction τ1^0 = 0.0105 Pa
Solid density ρ = 1.0 kg/m^3
Young's modulus E = 2.5 Pa
Poisson's ratio ν = 0.25
Wave velocities cp = 1.73 m/s and cs = 1.0 m/s
Periodic boundary condition replication length w = 40 m and domain height h = 20 m
Nucleation ellipse parameters aell = 0.6 m, bell = 3.6 m, vell = 0.825 m/s, and maximum contact pressure reduction α = 0.8
dependent_variables: Dynamic slip velocity |V|
Rupture front propagation speed Vr
Dynamic mesh convergence (relative error across total propagation distance and arrival time)
Regularised frictional strength τ1^s
Relative amplitude attenuation ratio A/A0
Critical regularisation characteristic length scale Lc

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Dynamic slip propagation along a deformable-rigid interface achieves mesh convergence in explicit finite-element simulations using Prakash-Clifton friction regularisation without introducing bulk or numerical damping.

A critical regularisation length scale exists below which decreasing the characteristic length no longer alters rupture front propagation, slip velocity, or rupture speed, causing the interface to behave as if governed by classical Coulomb friction.

The simplified Prakash-Clifton regularisation acts analytically as a temporal low-pass filter on contact stress perturbations, attenuating high-frequency oscillations with an amplitude ratio of A/A0 = 1 / sqrt(1 + (2*pi*f/C)^2).

Experimental identification of an interface's physical length scale requires dynamic slip pulses with sufficiently high frequency content exceeding a critical frequency; otherwise, the measured value reflects the event-dependent critical length rather than the physical interface property.

future_work: Investigating the existence and behavior of critical length scales for slip events propagating along more general deformable-deformable (bimaterial) interfaces.
Applying the proposed verification procedure to experimentally monitor slip pulses with rich high-frequency content to measure physical characteristic interface length scales.
independent_variables: Characteristic length scale of the friction regularisation (L)
Interface mesh discretisation / node density (nd)
Input perturbation frequency (f) in spectral analysis
limitations_inferred: The conclusions are derived from a simplified two-dimensional plane-strain model of an isotropic linear elastic solid sliding against a rigid flat plane, which may not directly represent 3D geometries, complex deformable-deformable contacts, or velocity-weakening friction laws.

Slip was initiated via an artificial spatio-temporal reduction of normal contact stress, which predetermines the initial frequency spectrum and could influence the apparent critical length scale compared to spontaneous natural nucleation.
Thermal effects, interface opening, material wear, and adhesive interactions at the contact interface were not incorporated into the formulation.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Experimental data for Prakash-Clifton regularisation parameters are lacking for most material pairings.

Physical characteristic length scales deduced from experimental friction measurements are on the order of micrometers, requiring extremely fine spatial discretisation and heavy computational effort in numerical simulations.
The analysis simplified the regularisation by fixing the reference velocity V⋆ while only varying the characteristic length L.

The problem configuration was intentionally limited to a well-posed regime (friction coefficient below unity and equal static and kinetic coefficients) to avoid confounding regularisation mechanics with ill-posed to well-posed transitions.
Interface opening was suppressed during nucleation by limiting normal pressure reductions to 80% of initial values.
The spectral study examined signal amplitude attenuation while neglecting phase offset analysis.
Physical length scales cannot be determined experimentally if the slip event's frequency content falls below the critical frequency.
main_results: Mesh convergence in dynamic finite-element sliding simulations was successfully achieved without bulk or numerical damping by using Prakash-Clifton friction regularisation.
A convergence map in the space of characteristic length (L) versus interface node density (nd) demonstrated that smaller regularisation lengths require increasingly fine mesh discretisation.

Identified a critical characteristic length (Lc = 10^-5 m for the analyzed system) below which the choice of L does not affect the local slip velocity, rupture front propagation, or steady rupture velocity.

Demonstrated via spectral analysis that the Prakash-Clifton regularisation behaves as a low-pass filter, attenuating high-frequency contact disturbances and eliminating spurious high-frequency oscillations.

Established that the domain of influence of friction regularisation is bounded by the regularisation length and the spectral frequency content of the slip event; frequencies below the critical frequency propagate effectively under Coulomb friction.
Formulated a four-step experimental guideline to verify whether monitored slip events contain sufficient high-frequency energy to extract true physical interface length scales.
modeling_methods: Finite-element method (FEM) with two-dimensional regular quadrilateral elements and linear interpolation (four integration points)
Explicit Newmark-beta time integration scheme with lumped mass matrix
Simplified Prakash-Clifton dynamic friction regularisation law
Laplace-transform-based steady-state frequency response / spectral analysis
performance_metrics: Mesh convergence criteria (relative error over total propagation distance below 0.5% and arrival time error below 0.1%)
Slip velocity amplitude and temporal profile
Rupture front velocity Vr
Critical characteristic length scale Lc
Output-to-input amplitude attenuation ratio A/A0
possible_gap_implications: In mechanical modeling of dynamic contact and friction (relevant to soft grippers, continuum robots, and flexible structures), numerical regularisation length scales must be calibrated against the system's operational frequency spectrum to avoid unphysical damping of slip dynamics.

Experimental mechanics studies aiming to characterize interfacial frictional properties and contact mechanics must utilize high-frequency dynamic sensing and sharp transient excitation to resolve micro-scale interface length parameters.
paper.research_objective: To investigate the influence of the simplified Prakash-Clifton friction regularisation on dynamic slip propagation at a deformable-rigid interface, establish mesh convergence requirements without bulk damping, demonstrate the existence of a critical regularisation length scale, and explain its behavior through spectral filter analysis.
paper.research_problem: Coulomb's friction law causes numerical instability and lack of mesh convergence in dynamic simulations of sliding interfaces, while interface regularisations introduce characteristic length scales whose mechanical influence on slip propagation and numerical convergence are not fully understood.
paper.title: The existence of a critical length scale in regularised friction

source.filename: 2015-Transition from stick to slip in Hertzian contact with.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Linear elastic behavior for the contacting bodies.
Elastic similarity between contacting bodies (Dundurs' parameter beta equals zero), decoupling normal pressure from shear traction distributions.
Poisson's ratio effects on transverse shear tractions are neglected, treating tangential energy release rate as pure mode II.
Initial contact gap is spherical/quadratic, consistent with Hertzian contact assumptions.
Coulomb friction law holds within the slip region with a constant sliding friction coefficient.
Slip initiation at the stick-slip boundary is governed by a Griffith energy release rate criterion / critical mode II stress intensity factor.
Direct normal adhesion is neglected, assuming classical normal adhesion is eliminated by surface roughness.
control_variables: Normalized tangential load ratio (Q / (f * P))
Dimensionless toughness parameter / critical stick size ratio (c_c / a or c_c0 / a)
Normal contact load (P)
Sphere contact radius (R)
Contact pressure ratio relative to reference pressure (p_0 / p_0,nom) in the pressure-dependent model
dependent_variables: Stick zone radius (c) and stick-to-contact radius ratio (c / a)
Shear traction distribution q_x(r) across the interface
Critical stick zone radius c_c (and pressure-corrected critical radius c_c')
Threshold tangential load to initiate microslip (Q_min)
Peak tangential load prior to global sliding instability (Q_max) / apparent static friction coefficient
Mode II stress intensity factor (K_II) at the stick-slip boundary

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The transition from stick to slip in Hertzian contact can be modeled by superposing Hertzian contact pressure and a mode II singular adhesive solution analogous to JKR theory, where slip inception follows a Griffith fracture criterion while sliding follows Coulomb friction.

The Griffith friction model predicts that the stick zone remains larger than predicted by classical Cattaneo-Mindlin theory and collapses abruptly into global sliding when reaching a critical stick zone size analogous to JKR pull-off.

The apparent static friction coefficient before sliding can significantly exceed the sliding friction coefficient, exhibiting size and normal load dependencies governed by the friction fracture energy.

Experimental measurements in PMMA interfaces show that local shear-to-normal stress ratios can reach values several times higher than the macroscopic static friction coefficient without precipitating slip, with strain fields consistent with shear crack fracture mechanics.
Incorporating a contact-pressure-dependent friction toughness accounts for variations in real contact area and alters the stick zone scaling across varying pressure regimes.

Historical experimental data for spherical contacts under oscillating tangential loads reveal stick zones 10-20% larger than classical Cattaneo-Mindlin predictions and non-cubic energy dissipation scaling, consistent with fracture mechanics-based stick-slip models.

future_work: Developing criteria to reliably select appropriate physical constants for cohesive/fracture models of friction from experimental data.
Extending the singular adhesive contact framework to more general non-axisymmetric contact geometries.
Further investigating whether interfacial roughness effects or fracture mechanics models better explain observed deviations in frictional energy dissipation under oscillating loads.
independent_variables: Tangential load (Q)
Normal contact load (P)
Contact radius (a) and sphere radius (R)
Mode II friction fracture energy (gamma) or nominal fracture energy (gamma_nom)
Radial position (r) within the contact area
Peak contact pressure (p_0)
limitations_inferred: The formulation is restricted to isotropic linear elastic materials and ideal spherical geometries, requiring modifications for compliant, viscoelastic, or highly deformable materials common in soft robotics.
The model assumes an idealized singular crack tip without an extended cohesive process zone, which may become inaccurate when stick zones approach asperity-scale dimensions.
Dynamic slip propagation velocity, interfacial wear, frictional heating, and slip-rate-dependent friction evolution are not modeled within this quasi-static framework.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The model is quasi-static and does not account for viscoelastic and dynamic effects observed during interfacial slip propagation.
The spherical contact geometry analyzed differs significantly from the flat, sharp-edged geometries typically used in laboratory friction experiments.
Poisson's ratio effects are neglected by assuming shear stresses act purely parallel to the applied tangential load direction.
Exact analytical formulation is straightforward only for axisymmetric contacts; elliptical and more complex geometries require approximations.
The choice of reference nominal fracture energy at peak pressure is arbitrary.
Estimating physical constants for cohesive or fracture models remains uncertain due to large discrepancies in measured local shear-to-normal stress ratios.
main_results: Complete stick is maintained up to a non-zero threshold tangential load (Q_min), unlike classical Cattaneo-Mindlin theory where microslip initiates immediately upon tangential loading.
Beyond the threshold load, the stick zone remains larger than the classical Cattaneo-Mindlin prediction for equivalent tangential loads.
When the stick region decreases to a critical size (c_c), force-controlled equilibrium becomes unstable, triggering a sudden transition to global sliding.

The peak tangential load prior to sliding can exceed the dynamic sliding limit (f * P) by up to a factor of 2 for partial-slip solutions, offering an explanation for the difference between static and dynamic friction coefficients.
Assuming constant friction fracture energy introduces contact size and normal load dependence into the apparent static friction coefficient.
Modifying the model with a pressure-dependent toughness retains the enlarged stick zone and critical drop to sliding, though the effect is attenuated at low pressures.
modeling_methods: Superposition method extending the Cattaneo-Mindlin tangential contact formulation.
Classical Hertzian contact pressure theory for spherical normal contact.
Mode II fracture mechanics formulation using the JKR adhesive contact solution for the corrective shear traction distribution in the stick zone.
Amontons-Coulomb friction law applied within the slip annulus.
Linearly pressure-dependent fracture toughness model accounting for real contact area variations.
Bounded asymptotic stress intensity factor analysis at the stick-slip boundary.
performance_metrics: Stick zone radius ratio (c / a)
Normalized tangential load ratio (Q / (f * P))
Normalized shear traction distribution (q_x / (f * p_0))
Critical stick zone radius ratio (c_c / a and c_c' / a)
Tangential load enhancement factor before global sliding (Q_max / (f * P))
Mode II stress intensity factor (K_II)
possible_gap_implications: Insights into the fracture-mechanics-governed transition from stick to slip and critical stick size instabilities could inform traction, grasping stability, and slip-onset models in compliant robotic grippers and contact interfaces, provided large deformations and viscoelasticity are incorporated.
Fracture mechanics descriptions of static friction enhancement and energy dissipation could improve contact compliance and fretting wear models in continuum joint mechanisms.
paper.research_objective: To formulate an analytical model for the Cattaneo-Mindlin problem of a Hertzian contact by introducing a Griffith fracture mechanics condition for the inception of slip in the stick region while preserving Coulomb friction in the slip region, investigating both constant and pressure-dependent friction fracture energy.
paper.research_problem: Classical Cattaneo-Mindlin theory based on Amontons-Coulomb friction predicts instantaneous microslip upon tangential loading and load-independent friction coefficients, which fails to capture fracture-mechanics-type singular shear stresses, elevated local friction ratios, stick-zone enlargement, and abrupt transitions from static to dynamic friction observed experimentally and in fault mechanics.
paper.title: Transition from stick to slip in Hertzian contact with “Griffith” friction: The Cattaneo–Mindlin problem revisited

source.filename: 2016-Friction Characteristics of CFRP Plates in Contact with.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Unidirectional CFRP plate is an orthotropic and anisotropic material for which classical Hertzian contact theory is not applicable
Polymers in the CFRP composite deform viscoelastically under tension and interfacial sliding, conforming to Howell's friction power law (T = a * N^b)
Contact normal stress is assumed uniformly distributed across the two symmetric 15 mm x 20 mm nominal contact interfaces
control_variables: CFRP plate specimen dimensions (1.2 mm thickness, 20 mm width, 580 mm length) and material properties (68% fiber volume, Sika CarboDur)
Contact interface area (15 mm length x 20 mm width on two opposing faces)
Copper plate thickness (0.8 mm)
Horizontal pullout displacement rate (25 mm/s)
Normal load application rate (2 kN/s) and pre-pull stabilization duration (30 s)
Pre-test surface cleaning protocol using isopropanol
Data acquisition rate (1,000 scans/s, averaged to ~200 scans per plot point)
dependent_variables: Static coefficient of friction
Interfacial shear stress
Horizontal pullout force
Maximum sliding distance before plate rupture or machine stroke limit
Interfacial wear and damage mechanisms (ploughing, debris accumulation, stick-slip behavior, tensile fiber fracture)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Under transverse contact pressures between 50 and 175 MPa, unidirectional CFRP plates sliding against copper follow viscoelastic friction models where softer annealed copper exhibits higher friction coefficients (0.39 to 0.30) than harder as-received copper (0.31) due to asperity deformation increasing the real contact area.

High normal contact pressures (150 to 175 MPa) during sliding cause severe ploughing, carbon debris accumulation, cross-sectional thickness shaving, and premature tensile fiber rupture of CFRP plates at loads well below their ultimate tensile strength.

Interfacial sliding between composite plates and copper counterfaces displays periodic stick-slip behavior at moderate normal pressures (50 to 100 MPa), governed by cyclic debris accumulation and release at the contact interface.

Interfacial shear stress versus normal contact pressure for composite-metal contact with a soft metal counterface can be described by a modified Howell power-law formulation (tau = 1.02 * sigma^0.76) reflecting pressure-dependent contact area growth.

experimental_setup: Friction test apparatus in a test machine utilizing two hardened steel clamping plates (45 HRC, 15 mm x 100 mm) to apply normal compressive load across a 15 mm x 20 mm contact zone on both sides of a CFRP plate
Unidirectional CFRP plate specimens (580 mm long, 20 mm wide, 1.2 mm thick, 68% fiber volume, epoxy matrix) pulled horizontally between two 0.8 mm thick copper plates
Annealed copper plates prepared by heat treatment in an oven at 500 deg C for 1 hour followed by air cooling to room temperature
Rockwell superficial microhardness testing (HR15TS scale, 15 kg mass, 1.59 mm diameter ball) to characterize material hardness of CFRP and copper plates
Built-in LVDT and 44.5 kN load cell measuring displacement and horizontal force at a 25 mm/s displacement rate and 2 kN/s normal loading rate
future_work: Utilization of CFRP-copper friction parameters for the design and development of novel friction-based wedge anchors for composite plates in structural rehabilitation and retrofitting
Application of friction data to the design of lightweight composite components in automotive, aviation, space, and shipbuilding industries
Development of innovative composite materials combining carbon fibers, resin matrix, and copper
Use of the experimental data as a benchmark for other composite-to-metal contact configurations of similar geometry
independent_variables: Copper plate condition and hardness (as-received at 67 HR15TS vs. annealed at 34 HR15TS)
Applied normal contact stress (50, 75, 100, 125, 150, and 175 MPa)
limitations_inferred: Experiments were conducted solely under dry ambient laboratory conditions, without assessing temperature variations, humidity, or environmental degradation
Only a single pullout displacement rate (25 mm/s) was tested, so rate-dependent viscoelastic effects and frictional heating across varying velocities were not characterized
The investigation is limited to flat unidirectional CFRP plates sliding against copper, meaning findings cannot be directly applied to multidirectional laminates or other metal pairings
The research focuses strictly on structural engineering anchor systems and does not investigate robotic mechanisms, soft actuators, or compliant systems
limitations_stated_by_authors: Friction behavior above 175 MPa contact pressure could not be evaluated within scope because CFRP plates ruptured in tension after 30 to 50 mm displacement prior to reaching peak load
Initial slippage occurred at the non-testing end of the smooth CFRP plate inside machine grips, necessitating epoxying copper plates to the gripping tabs
Cutting 100-mm-wide stock CFRP plates into 20-mm-wide test specimens severed side fibers, resulting in a reduction of the plate tensile strength
Maximum allowable sliding distance was restricted to 98 mm by the stroke limit of the friction test machine
main_results: For as-received copper plates, the shear stress versus normal contact pressure was linear (tau = 0.31 * sigma, R^2 = 0.97) with a constant coefficient of friction of 0.31 across 50 to 175 MPa normal stress

For annealed copper plates, the coefficient of friction decreased from 0.39 at 50 MPa to 0.30 at 175 MPa, following a power-law relationship (tau = 1.02 * sigma^0.76, R^2 = 0.92) consistent with Howell's friction model for viscoelastic materials

Softer annealed copper exhibited higher friction coefficients and peak horizontal forces than harder as-received copper between 50 and 150 MPa due to greater real contact area from asperity deformation
Maximum sliding distance before failure decreased with increasing contact pressure for both copper conditions

Stick-slip sliding behavior occurred at 50 to 100 MPa due to debris buildup and clearing cycles, whereas at 150 to 175 MPa, severe ploughing and cross-sectional shaving resulted in tensile rupture at 28 to 34 kN
modeling_methods: Empirical linear contact friction modeling using Amonton's law (tau = 0.31 * sigma) for as-received copper plates
Empirical power-law contact friction modeling based on Howell's formulation for viscoelastic materials (tau = 1.02 * sigma^0.76) for annealed copper plates
Double-interface friction formulation relating total horizontal pullout force, normal force, shear stress, and contact stress (mu = Tmax / (2 * N) = tau / sigma)
performance_metrics: Static coefficient of friction (mu)
Interfacial shear stress (MPa)
Maximum sliding distance before failure (mm)
Horizontal breaking force / tensile rupture load (kN)
possible_gap_implications: Tribological modeling and experimental mechanics of high-pressure composite-to-soft-metal contact can inform the mechanical design of high-force tendon anchors, rigid-compliant couplings, and clamping mechanisms in heavy-duty continuum or robotic structures where preventing transverse shear crushing is crucial.

Because this study investigates civil structural anchors under high pressures (50 to 175 MPa), there is an unaddressed research gap in evaluating composite-metal contact mechanics under the lower-pressure, large-displacement, highly compliant regimes typical of soft robotics and soft grippers.
paper.research_objective: To experimentally determine the coefficient of friction, shear stress versus normal stress relationship, sliding mechanisms, and wear behavior between unidirectional CFRP plates and two types of copper plates (as-received and annealed) under high contact pressures from 50 to 175 MPa.
paper.research_problem: Lack of coefficient of friction data and tribological characterization for unidirectional CFRP plates in contact with copper under high contact pressure, which is necessary for designing friction-based anchors that protect CFRP plates from transverse shear failure.
paper.title: Friction Characteristics of CFRP Plates in Contact with Copper Plates under High Contact Pressure

source.filename: 2021-A full layered numerical model for predicting hysteretic behavior of unbonded flexible pipes considering initial contact pressure.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Plane sections remain plane assumption applied for curvature calculation from measured outer fiber strains.
Isotropic linear elastic material behavior for polymeric sheath layers, tapes, and steel tensile armor tendons.
Equivalent orthotropic linear elastic shell formulation for carcass and pressure zeta armor layers, with negligible longitudinal elastic modulus to reflect negligible longitudinal bending stiffness.
Coulomb friction model for tangential contact interactions between adjacent layers.
Hard contact penalty method formulation for normal contact behavior between layers.
Pipe length is assumed to remain unchanged during bending cycles because axial elongation under internal pressure is small relative to cantilever length.
Initial contact pressure is assumed to originate from outer sheath shrinkage during thermal cool-down in the manufacturing process.
control_variables: Flexible pipe structural geometry and layer dimensions (101.6 mm inner diameter, 9 concentric layers).
Tensile armor tendon cross-section dimensions (5 mm x 2 mm) and wound lay angle (+/-38 degrees).
Sinusoidal loading frequency of 0.1 Hz for cyclic bending.
Room temperature testing environment.
Cantilever beam span of 1.35 m from clamped point to load cell point and moment arm of 1.19 m to measurement gauge.
Finite element model length of 1350 mm (approximately 2.26 times the pitch length of the outer tensile armor layer).
Zero external effective tension applied during internal pressurization.
dependent_variables: Bending moment at the measurement location
Curvature distribution along the pipe length
Bending moment-curvature hysteretic response (stick stiffness, slip stiffness, and friction moment)
Tensile armor tendon local stress components (axial stress, transverse bending stress, and normal bending stress)
True wall tension and reaction forces and moments at pipe ends
Numerical simulation time and computational resource requirements

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Full-scale displacement-controlled cantilever bending tests on a 4-inch unbonded flexible pipe demonstrate hysteretic bending behavior driven by internal interlayer slip, where curvature at the gauge location decreases as internal pressure increases under a constant displacement amplitude.

A predefined stress field method prescribing a 2 MPa hoop stress in the outer sheath accurately simulates manufacturing-induced initial contact pressure and reproduces experimental bending moment-curvature hysteretic curves across 0.7 MPa, 10 MPa, and 20 MPa internal pressures without reducing true wall tension.

Helical tensile armor tendons under cyclic bending undergo stick, transition, and slip phases that initiate at the neutral bending axis and progress toward the intrados and extrados, sliding in an intermediate path between geodesic and loxodromic trajectories.

Modeling polymeric layers using solid elements (C3D8I) produces higher friction moments than using shell elements (S4R) because Poisson's effect increases tendon mean axial stress and interlayer contact force during pipe elongation.

experimental_setup: Full-scale 101.6 mm (4 inch) 9-layer rough-bore unbonded flexible pipe specimen of 8 m total length tested at MARINTEK (SINTEF Ocean) in 1991 by Skallerud.
Cantilever beam setup created by clamping two halves of steel tubes (EndA) onto the pipe 1.35 m from the load cell point (EndB).
Two extensometers (10 mm gauge length, +/-10% maximum strain range) attached on opposite outer fibers 1.19 m from EndB to measure bending curvature under plane-sections-remain-plane assumption.
Displacement-controlled cyclic bending via a force actuator connected to the end flange through a thin steel plate to eliminate secondary bending moments.
Sinusoidal loading signal with 0.1 Hz frequency and 70 mm prescribed displacement amplitude tested at 0.7 MPa, 10 MPa, and 20 MPa internal pressure at room temperature without axial tension.
future_work: Investigate the applicability and transferability of the 2 MPa predefined stress value to other unbonded flexible pipe configurations and dimensions.
Incorporate additional sources of initial contact pressure, such as residual stresses generated during the manufacturing and forming of tensile armor tendons.
independent_variables: Internal pressure level (0.7 MPa, 10 MPa, 20 MPa).
Outer sheath predefined stress level (2 MPa, 5 MPa, 10 MPa).
Initial contact pressure modeling approach (predefined stress fields / prestress method, conventional external pressure / ep method, effective tension / teff method).
Element formulation for polymeric sheath layers (solid elements C3D8I vs. shell elements S4R).
Interlayer friction coefficients (varied across 0.05 to 0.35, specifically 0.21, 0.23, and 0.26 for tested pressure cases).
Tendon mesh refinement and element formulation (C3D8R vs. C3D8I with varying thickness, width, and length divisions).
Boundary condition formulations at clamped tubes point EndA (encastre vs. spring elements) and load cell point EndB (degrees of freedom combinations).
Material property formulation of wound anti-wear and structural tapes (isotropic shell vs. orthotropic shell).
Interlayer normal contact stiffness specification (default penalty contact stiffness vs. analytical formula stiffness).
limitations_inferred: The model was validated solely against quasi-static cyclic bending data from a single 4-inch pipe geometry and was not evaluated under multi-axial dynamic bending, torsion, or coupled fluid-thermal loads.
The study investigates marine unbonded flexible pipes and does not examine or demonstrate applicability to soft robotics, continuum robots, or robotic grippers.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The calibrated predefined stress value of 2 MPa was determined for the specific pipe studied and requires further investigation to assess applicability to other flexible pipe designs.
Other contributing sources of initial contact pressure, particularly residual stresses induced during the manufacturing of tensile armor tendons, were not modeled.
Detailed geometric profiles of the carcass and pressure zeta armor layers were not reported in the benchmark test and had to be estimated using iterative correction methods.
Equivalent orthotropic shell representations of carcass and pressure zeta layers create geometric gaps that necessitate artificial filling layers with negligible stiffness.
main_results: The predefined stress fields method with a 2 MPa hoop prestress in the outer sheath successfully matched experimental moment-curvature hysteresis loops across low, intermediate, and high internal pressure levels (0.7 MPa, 10 MPa, 20 MPa).

The conventional external pressure method artificially compressed the pipe and lowered true wall tension, reducing tendon mean axial stress and risking numerical buckling, which was avoided by the predefined stress method.
Tensile armor tendons slide in an interval between theoretical loxodromic and geodesic curves, as confirmed by non-zero transverse bending stresses.
Tendon slip initiates at the neutral bending axis where shear stress exceeds capacity and spreads toward the intrados and extrados with increasing curvature.
Cantilever boundary conditions at clamped location EndA can be modeled as encastre in Abaqus without requiring spring elements to represent the remaining 6.65 m pipe span.
Modeling polymeric sheath layers with solid elements results in larger friction moments than shell elements due to Poisson's ratio effects on pipe elongation.
Friction coefficients exceeding 0.2 trigger unsymmetric solver algorithms in Abaqus/Standard, substantially increasing runtime and computational resource demands.
modeling_methods: Full-layered 3D finite element modeling using the implicit solver of Abaqus/Standard under quasi-static conditions.
Equivalent orthotropic shell modeling (S4R elements) for the interlocked carcass and pressure zeta armor layers with tuned directional stiffnesses.
Incompatible mode 8-node hexahedral solid elements (C3D8I) for tensile armor tendons to eliminate shear locking and hourglassing.
Surface-to-surface (S2S) penalty contact formulation with Coulomb friction and hard normal contact.
Predefined stress fields method applied as initial hoop stress in the outer sheath to model manufacturing-induced contact pressure.
Filling surface layers (SFM3D4 elements) with negligible stiffness to close gaps between equivalent shell layers and adjacent polymeric sheaths.
Rigid body end fittings (R3D4 elements) coupled to reference points to accurately capture internal pressure endcap effects.
Centrally located dummy beam element (B31) with negligible stiffness to extract curvature distribution along the pipe length.
performance_metrics: Stick bending stiffness (slope of linear elastic stick zone)
Slip bending stiffness (slope of full slip zone)
Friction moment / hysteretic loop width
Maximum bending moment at prescribed curvature
Cross-sectional curvature at the gauge location and curvature distribution along pipe length
Local axial stress (sigma_xx-ax), transverse bending stress (sigma_xx-my), and normal bending stress (sigma_xx-mz) in tendons
CPU simulation runtime and computational resource utilization
possible_gap_implications: The predefined stress field formulation and interlayer stick-slip friction contact modeling could provide foundational mechanics insights for modeling multi-layered flexible continuum structures or friction-based variable stiffness mechanisms, though validation in soft robotics is currently absent.

Accounting for Poisson's ratio effects in thick compliant polymer sheaths under axial elongation may be critical for accurately predicting friction-induced hysteretic bending stiffness in multi-layered soft robotic segments.
paper.research_objective: Develop a full-layered 3D numerical model of an unbonded flexible pipe using the implicit solver of Abaqus to predict quasi-static bending hysteretic behavior, introduce a predefined stress fields method on the outer sheath to account for manufacturing-induced initial contact pressure without sacrificing true wall tension, validate the model against full-scale 4-inch pipe bending test data across multiple internal pressure levels, allow unconstrained slip paths of tensile armor tendons, and evaluate sensitivity to key modeling parameters.
paper.research_problem: Predicting the non-linear bending hysteretic behavior and interlayer stress states of unbonded flexible pipes subjected to internal pressure and cyclic bending, while accurately accounting for initial contact pressure from manufacturing without causing artificial axial pipe compression (true wall tension reduction) and avoiding explicit solver drawbacks like mass scaling and dynamic vibration.
paper.title: A full layered numerical model for predicting hysteretic behavior of unbonded flexible pipes considering initial contact pressure

Time-harmonic wave motion with angular frequency omega
Stress-free traction boundary conditions at outer surfaces of the laminate waveguide
Continuity of traction vectors across internal layer interfaces
Imperfect interface modeled via effective spring boundary conditions (ESBC) with a diagonal spring stiffness matrix where normal and tangential stiffnesses are equal (kappa_11 = kappa_22 = kappa)
Quasi-static approximation for interface micro-cracks where defect width is much smaller than the wavelength (l << lambda)
Substrate layer of the retro-reflective tape assumed to be mechanically identical to the epoxy film

Adhesive layer thickness (40 um two-sided epoxy tape)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Effective spring boundary conditions (ESBC) expressing spring stiffness in terms of material moduli and micro-crack geometry can quantitatively and qualitatively model guided wave dispersion changes in multi-layered laminates with damaged interfaces.

Different guided wave modes show different sensitivity to interface degradation: even-numbered modes (GW2, GW4, GW6) exhibit significantly greater shifts in slowness with decreasing spring stiffness than odd-numbered modes (GW1, GW3, GW5).

For aluminium-epoxy laminates with mechanical surface scratches, ESBC stiffness was experimentally evaluated in the range 40-60 GPa/mm (Cl = 0.01-0.02 mm), matching manufacturing estimates (Cl = 0.005-0.015 mm).
For laminates with strip-like knife cuts at the interface, ESBC stiffness was experimentally identified between 2 and 4 GPa/mm (Cl = 0.25-0.5 mm), matching measured crack geometry (Cl = 0.1-0.4 mm).

Severe abrasive degradation of the adhesive film using emery led to spring stiffness kappa < 1 GPa/mm (Cl > 0.35 mm), causing guided wave slownesses to approach the behavior of a fully debonded interface.

experimental_setup: Three-layered laminate specimens consisting of two 2 mm-thick aluminium plates bonded with a 40 um-thick two-sided epoxy tape, cured for 24 h at room temperature under 1600 Pa pressure

Four interface conditions investigated: pristine/undamaged interface, lower epoxy surface partially abraded with emery, upper aluminium surface scratched with a wire brush, and upper aluminium surface notched with strip-like knife cuts (0.2-0.5 mm wide)
Circular piezoelectric actuators (PZT PIC 151, 10 mm diameter, 0.5 mm thick) adhesively mounted to excite elastodynamic guided waves
Polytec PSV-500-V laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) positioned 1100 mm above the specimen scanning out-of-plane surface velocity along a central line
3M 7610 Scotchlite high gain retro-reflective sheeting strip (100 um thick) applied along the LDV scanning path to enhance signal-to-noise ratio
Plasticine applied around the specimen borders to minimize edge boundary reflections
future_work: Extending the ESBC methodology to account for other micro-defect geometries such as circular, elliptical, or rectangular cracks using alternative stiffness relations
Applying the modeling framework to more complex composite materials and anisotropic media
independent_variables: Type and severity of interfacial damage (intact/perfect contact, wire brush scratches, strip-like cuts, and emery-damaged adhesive)
Excitation wave frequency (evaluated in the range 0.1 MHz to 0.8 MHz)
Spatial position x1 along the specimen surface measurement line
limitations_inferred: The investigation is restricted to planar two-dimensional wave propagation and simple flat specimen geometries, not addressing complex 3D structures or curved components
Manual defect fabrication techniques (knife cutting, wire brush scratching, emery sanding) generate non-uniform crack geometry and spacing across the interface
The paper evaluates static manufactured damage in structural metals/epoxy laminates and does not investigate soft robotic materials, elastomers, or active variable-stiffness devices
limitations_stated_by_authors: Analytical expressions for spring stiffness (Eqs. 5 and 6) strictly apply only to planar arrays of strip-like micro-cracks oriented perpendicular to wave propagation and are not strictly valid for non-aligned random scratch patterns
The quasi-static approximation parameter zeta(f) is frequency-dependent in reality, decreasing by up to 50% as frequency increases
Different defect shapes (circular, elliptical) require distinct formulations for effective interfacial spring stiffnesses
The retro-reflective tape substrate was simplified as mechanically identical to the epoxy layer in the numerical waveguide model
main_results: Experimental validation demonstrated that ESBC accurately captures the changes in guided wave dispersion caused by imperfect and degraded laminate interfaces

Estimated interfacial spring stiffnesses matched theoretical calculations based on physical crack density and width measurements (scratched aluminium: kappa = 40-60 GPa/mm; strip cuts: kappa = 2-4 GPa/mm; abraded adhesive: kappa < 1 GPa/mm)
Guided wave mode GW2 was particularly sensitive to slight surface scratching, while GW3 shifted markedly toward debonded behavior under severe interface degradation
The contact degradation severity in multi-layer structures can be classified and quantitatively reconstructed through frequency-wavenumber analysis combined with ESBC
modeling_methods: Lamé elastodynamic differential formulation for in-plane wave propagation in multi-layered isotropic waveguides
Effective spring boundary conditions (ESBC) specifying stress traction continuity and displacement jump proportional to interfacial spring stiffness (tau = kappa * [u])
Spatial Fourier transform with respect to coordinate x1 to convert the governing partial differential equations into ordinary differential equations and establish linear dispersion algebraic systems
Quasi-static micromechanical modeling (Baik-Thompson and Lekesiz-Katsube-Rokhlin-Seghi models) relating spring stiffness to crack density, average defect width, and elastic constants
Two-dimensional Fourier transform frequency-wavenumber analysis (FWA) of measured surface velocity profiles to extract experimental dispersion curves
performance_metrics: Guided wave slowness s (us/m) as a function of frequency f (MHz)
Interfacial spring stiffness kappa (GPa/mm)
Damage parameter product Cl (crack density C multiplied by average defect width l, mm)
Agreement/discrepancy between theoretical and experimental dispersion curves
possible_gap_implications: The ESBC framework could potentially provide a theoretical and experimental basis for modeling interfacial compliance or bond degradation between flexible composite layers or bonded soft-rigid interfaces

Guided wave inspection with ESBC could potentially be adapted for non-destructive health evaluation of laminated flexible components, though high material damping in soft elastomers remains an unexamined challenge

paper.research_problem: Accurate non-destructive evaluation and mechanical modeling of interfacial degradation and weakened adhesion in adhesively bonded multi-layered laminate structures using ultrasonic guided waves and effective spring boundary conditions.
paper.title: Experimental validation of the applicability of effective spring boundary conditions for modelling damaged interfaces in laminate structures

constitutive_assumptions: Quasi-static conditions, infinitesimal deformation, and absence of body forces in the continuum formulation.
Linear elastic isotropic bulk material behavior governed by Hooke's law.
Classical Coulomb friction law modified by a C1-continuous smoothing function of tangential slip displacement.
C2-continuous truncated logarithmic barrier energy density function for interface normal contact pressure.
Two-dimensional single and stationary embedded interfaces under plane-strain conditions.

Interface friction coefficient (μ)
Domain dimensions and interface geometry/orientation
Boundary displacement and traction loading increments
Finite element type (quadrilateral elements with linear shape functions)

Tangential slip displacement (uT)
Normal contact pressure (pN)
Tangential traction and shear stress (tT, τ)
Newton-Raphson iteration residual and convergence rate
Relative error norms of interface contact pressure solutions
Spurious oscillations in interface traction fields

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A smooth barrier energy function enforces non-penetration contact constraints on embedded interfaces without introducing additional degrees of freedom or ill-conditioned matrices.

A continuous friction smoothing function describes the stick-slip transition smoothly, providing numerical robustness and quadratic Newton convergence during mixed stick-slip contact where standard penalty methods fail.
An averaged surface integration scheme projecting displacement jumps onto a constant space mitigates spurious traction oscillations in enriched finite element contact surfaces.

Numerical simulations of contact between blocks with extreme stiffness contrast (up to 10^7) demonstrated quadratic convergence and non-oscillatory interface tractions using the barrier method with smoothed friction.

Verification against an analytical benchmark for circular inclusion separation confirmed asymptotic error convergence and effective oscillation suppression with the averaged surface integration scheme.

future_work: Extending the barrier formulation to three-dimensional embedded interface geometries.
Incorporating evolving or propagating interfaces and crack growth.
Adapting the framework to handle more sophisticated friction laws beyond standard Coulomb friction.
Extending the barrier method to other enriched or embedded numerical frameworks such as the extended material point method (XMPM).
independent_variables: Barrier thickness parameter defining maximum allowable separation gap (d̂)
Maximum microslip displacement parameter (ŝ)
Barrier stiffness parameter (κ)
Initial interface gap distance for closed interfaces (d0)
Approximated initial optimal contact pressure ((pN,0)optimal)
Mesh element size (h) across mesh refinement levels
Bulk material stiffness contrast ratio (Ehard / Esoft)
Applied boundary displacements and external normal and tangential tractions
Integration scheme (standard two-point Gauss quadrature versus averaged surface integration)
limitations_inferred: The formulation was evaluated exclusively through synthetic two-dimensional numerical benchmarks without experimental physical validation.
The applicability to nonlinear hyperelastic or viscoelastic materials (such as elastomers typically used in soft robotics) was not investigated.
The parameterization relies on an estimate of the initial contact pressure, which may be non-trivial to estimate in complex heterogeneous geometries or irregular loading conditions.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The study is strictly limited in scope to single and stationary interfaces in two dimensions.
The barrier formulation inherently prevents contact surfaces from being perfectly closed, enforcing a microscopic separation gap.
When the standard integration scheme does not generate traction oscillations, the averaged surface integration scheme is sub-optimal in terms of accuracy.
Newton iterations may fail to converge during early load steps if the initial optimal contact pressure estimate is chosen too low.
Extending the method to three-dimensional or evolving interface geometries requires substantial additional algorithmic developments.
main_results: The barrier method strictly satisfies the non-penetration constraint (uN > 0) without permitting inter-penetration, and allows direct control over maximum separation error via d̂.
A parameterization strategy setting d0 = 0.376 d̂ and κ = (pN,0)optimal / (2.256 d̂) optimizes Jacobian matrix conditioning and enables parameter-tuning-free implementation.

The smoothed friction law eliminates discontinuous derivatives in the tangent operator, enabling asymptotically quadratic Newton convergence in mixed stick-slip problems where penalty methods diverge.

The averaged surface integration scheme effectively suppresses spurious traction oscillations in embedded finite elements, achieving asymptotic convergence comparable to analytical and Lagrange multiplier solutions.
The formulation achieves these improvements while maintaining a low computational cost practically identical to the classical penalty method.
modeling_methods: Extended Finite Element Method (XFEM) with Heaviside jump enrichment for embedded discontinuities
Smooth barrier energy density function for contact constraint enforcement
C1-continuous smoothed Coulomb friction law with microslip formulation
Averaged surface integration scheme (weak penalty projection) for traction stabilization
Newton-Raphson iteration with direct linear solvers for discrete nonlinear variational systems
performance_metrics: Non-penetration constraint satisfaction (absence of over-closure / inter-penetration)
Accuracy and error norms of normal contact pressure and shear traction compared to analytical and reference solutions
Asymptotic convergence rate of Newton iterations (quadratic convergence behavior)
Mesh refinement convergence of normal and slip displacement jumps and interface tractions
Presence or suppression of spurious oscillations in interface traction fields
Conditioning of the Jacobian system matrix
possible_gap_implications: The barrier method and smoothed friction approach provide an efficient, oscillation-free modeling technique for frictional interfaces that could be relevant to simulating contact, sliding, or layer interactions in mechanical systems.

Because the barrier method guarantees strictly non-negative interface separation gaps, it is well-suited for coupled multiphysics modeling (such as fluid-structure interaction in embedded fluid channels or chambers).

The current restriction to linear elastic bulk materials and infinitesimal strains highlights a research gap for extending barrier contact algorithms to large-deformation, hyperelastic mechanics relevant to soft robotics.
paper.research_objective: To develop the first barrier method for frictional contact on embedded interfaces in finite elements (using XFEM) that eliminates inter-penetration, prevents ill-conditioned matrices, smooths stick-slip transitions, suppresses traction oscillations via an averaged surface integration scheme, and enables parameter-tuning-free application.
paper.research_problem: Existing contact algorithms for interfaces embedded in finite elements suffer from notable drawbacks: the penalty method permits unconstrained inter-penetration and causes ill-conditioning when penalty parameters are enlarged; the Lagrange multiplier method introduces additional degrees of freedom and inf-sup stability issues; and classical friction formulations cause non-convergence and traction oscillations during stick-slip transitions.
paper.title: A barrier method for frictional contact on embedded interfaces

Equivalent isotropic polymeric representation for the outer core layer
Hertz contact theory for evaluating spatial distance and contact angle between tensile armor tendons and helix contact beams
Coulomb friction model with penalty formulation and defined elastic slip tolerance
Loxodromic and geodesic curves as bounding kinematic paths for armor tendon bending stresses
Constant interlayer contact pressure assumption during bending deformation in analytical formulations

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Unbonded flexible pipes exhibit nonlinear bending hysteretic behavior governed by interlayer friction and contact pressure between tensile armor tendons and supporting layers, transitioning through stick, transition, and slip states.
evidence_relevant_to_topic.evidence_type: mechanical modeling and experimental data comparison

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A double helix contact beam model using node-to-surface contact discretization with Hertz contact angles accurately replicates the hysteretic bending moment-curvature response of full surface-to-surface FE models while reducing computational elements by 59 percent and runtime by up to 95 to 98 percent.

Accounting for initial interlayer contact pressure (via predefined hoop stress in the outer sheath) is essential for capturing the bending hysteretic loop and dissipated energy observed experimentally at low internal pressure levels (0.7 MPa).
evidence_relevant_to_topic.evidence_type: analytical and numerical model validation against experiments

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Tensile armor tendons slide along a path intermediate between loxodromic and geodesic curves, evidenced by non-zero transverse slip displacements and non-zero transverse bending stresses under cyclic bending.

The shear stiffness of supporting plastic layers significantly softens the initial stick bending stiffness compared to plane section models, and treating adjacent steel armor layers as boundary conditions yields stick stiffness matching experimental results.

experimental_setup: Cantilever full-scale cyclic bending test setup of a 4-inch rough-bore unbonded flexible pipe reported by Skallerud (1991)
Prescribed cyclic transverse displacement applied to the pipe end at a loading frequency of 0.1 Hz across 10 complete cycles to an amplitude curvature of 1/9 m^-1
Tests conducted under multiple internal pressure levels (0.7 MPa for test No. 3, 10 MPa for test No. 4, and 20 MPa for test No. 5)
future_work: Extension of the efficient cross-section contact modeling strategy to global dynamic analysis of flexible risers
Application of the predicted maximum total axial stress distributions to fatigue damage evaluation of tensile armor tendons
independent_variables: Internal pressure level (0.7 MPa, 10 MPa, 20 MPa)
Applied pipe curvature and prescribed bending displacement
Contact modeling method (full surface-to-surface contact vs. double helix contact beam method)
Layer representation (full individual layers vs. equivalent core layers)
Initial predefined residual stress in the outer sheath (0 MPa vs. 2 MPa) and residual strain in helical tendons
Helix contact beam contact angle parameter (phi, phi/2, phi/4, phi/8, phi/100, phi_Hertz) and beam element type (B31, B31H, B32, B32H, B33, B33H)
Tensile armor cross-section mesh density (1x1, 2x2, 3x3, 4x4)
Elastic slip tolerance in penalty friction formulation (0.005 down to 1e-5)
Combinations of plastic layer shear stiffness parameters in shear interaction models
limitations_inferred: The proposed equivalent double helix model was calibrated and validated against only a single 4-inch pipe geometry under pure bending and internal pressure; its generalization to larger pipe diameters or combined multi-axial loads (e.g., tension, torsion, and bending simultaneously) remains to be demonstrated.
The predefined residual stress value of 2 MPa is an empirical calibration parameter rather than a directly measured physical quantity for the specific pipe specimen.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Node-to-surface discretization in the helix contact beam model exhibits more severe local normal contact penetration than surface-to-surface contact, leading to localized beam deformations and deviations in normal bending stress and transverse slip displacements.

Analytical models assume constant interlayer contact pressure during bending, which causes analytical friction moments and hysteresis loops to exceed numerical predictions at higher internal pressures.

Equivalent core layered models with helix contact beams show higher cross-sectional ovalization than full surface-to-surface models due to the linking mode between helix contact beams and supporting layers.
Default elastic slip tolerance in Abaqus (0.005) is excessively large and causes underestimation of stick stiffness and friction moment unless reduced below 1e-3.
main_results: The equivalent layered double helix contact beam model (EQUI_SHCONT2B) decreased total elements by 59 percent, nodes by 43 percent, degrees of freedom by 42 percent, simulation time by 95 to 98 percent, and memory usage by 95 percent relative to the full surface-to-surface model.

Predicted bending moment-curvature hysteretic curves across 10 complete cycles closely agreed with full-scale experimental measurements and full layered numerical models for both low (0.7 MPa) and high (20 MPa) internal pressures.

Initial interlayer contact pressure significantly affects the hysteresis loop and energy dissipation at low internal pressure (0.7 MPa), but has a minor relative effect at high internal pressure (20 MPa) where axisymmetric pressure dominates.
Analytical shear interaction models with boundary conditions defined at adjacent steel armor layers accurately capture stick stiffness, whereas plane section models overestimate stick stiffness.
Tensile armor tendons exhibit both transverse bending stress and transverse relative slip, confirming they slide along an intermediate path between geodesic and loxodromic trajectories.
modeling_methods: Equivalent layered finite element modeling in Abaqus/Standard using an implicit solver
Double helix contact beam model (SHCONT2B) using B31 beam elements with node-to-surface contact discretization and hard normal penalty formulation
Equivalent stiffness core layer formulation (orthotropic shell for inner core, isotropic shell for outer core)
Closed-form thick-walled cylindrical shell theory (isotropic and orthotropic) for axisymmetric interlayer contact pressure calculation
Helical layer mechanical equilibrium and geometric compatibility formulations accounting for fill factors, residual strain, local bending, and torsion
Bending analytical models based on plane surfaces remain plane assumption and shear interaction assumption with return-mapping stick-slip formulations
Hertz contact theory for determining contact half-width and contact angles for helix contact beams
performance_metrics: Bending stick stiffness (slope in stick zone) and slip bending stiffness
Bending friction moment and hysteretic dissipated energy (hysteresis loop area)
Tensile armor tendon stress components: axial friction stress, normal bending stress, transverse bending stress, and maximum total axial stress
Tangential and transverse relative slip displacements
Cross-section ovality ratio e = (D_max - D_min) / (D_max + D_min)
Total element count, node count, and total variables (degrees of freedom)
Computational simulation runtime (hours) for internal pressure and bending cycles, and memory consumption (GB)
possible_gap_implications: Demonstrates that high-fidelity prediction of nonlinear friction hysteresis and local stresses in complex multi-layer flexible structures does not require computationally prohibitive 3D surface contact meshes, offering a practical pathway for global dynamic simulations.
Highlights the necessity of including manufacturing/initial residual stresses in contact models to avoid non-conservative stiffness and damping estimations at low operational tensions.
paper.research_objective: To develop an efficient equivalent layered contact numerical model using a double helix contact beam approach combined with an equivalent core strategy in Abaqus/Standard, alongside closed-form axisymmetric and bending analytical models that account for initial interlayer contact pressure and shear interactions to accurately and efficiently predict the bending hysteretic behavior, local stresses, and slip of unbonded flexible pipes.
paper.research_problem: Predicting the nonlinear bending hysteretic behavior, local stresses, and interlayer slip of unbonded flexible pipes using full-layered 3D finite element models with surface-to-surface contact algorithms is computationally onerous and resource-intensive, while existing analytical and numerical models often neglect or improperly treat the initial interlayer contact pressure effect.

shear interaction / shear deformation of supporting plastic layers
structural stiffness of concentric helical and cylindrical metallic and polymeric layers

constitutive_assumptions: Layers are composed of the same homogeneous, linearly elastic, and orthotropic material with principal material axes aligned with geometric axes.
Small displacements, rotations, and strains are assumed.
Plane strain conditions prevail parallel to the x2-x3 plane.
Transverse normal stresses are assumed to be negligible compared to other stress components and set to zero (sigma_33 = 0) in the kinematic equilibrium formulation.

Interfaces between adjacent layers are treated as continuous zero-thickness mathematical surfaces where relative sliding is permitted but relative transverse normal separation or penetration is forbidden.
Interfacial sliding displacements and interfacial shear tractions follow a linear constitutive relationship governed by tangential stiffness coefficients.
Residual stresses from manufacturing and thermal stresses from environmental gradients are neglected.
control_variables: Beam length L and thickness h with length-to-thickness aspect ratio L/h = 5
Uniform layer thickness (t = h/n for n = 2 and n = 3)
Lamina orthotropic elastic properties: EL, ET = EL/25, GLT = EL/50, GTT = EL/125, and Poisson's ratios nuLT = nuTT = 0.25
Shear correction factor k44 = 5/6
Mid-thickness reference surface (x3 = 0)
Simply supported boundary conditions at x2 = 0 and x2 = L
Zero transverse normal displacement jump at layer interfaces
dependent_variables: Primal fictitious bending displacement w0b
Global kinematic variables: longitudinal displacement v02, transverse displacement w0, and rotation phi2
Local layer longitudinal displacements (k)v2
Local layer bending normal stresses (k)sigma22
Local layer transverse shear stresses (k)sigma23 computed a posteriori from local equilibrium
Interfacial displacement jumps and shear tractions across adjacent layers
Stress and moment resultants N22, Q22, M22, and MZS22

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A homogenized zigzag theory enables modeling multi-layered beams with imperfect sliding interfaces as equivalent single layers, reducing degrees of freedom compared to layerwise discrete theories.

Decoupling the three displacement unknowns of the zigzag model into a single sixth-order ordinary differential equation in a fictitious bending variable circumvents shear-locking issues in numerical discretization schemes.

Decreasing interfacial tangential stiffness increases layer compliance, creating pronounced jumps in longitudinal displacements and bending stresses and increasing overall displacement magnitudes relative to perfectly bonded configurations.

As interfacial tangential stiffness increases to sufficiently high thresholds (K_S*h/ET = 10 for two-layer beams and 5 for three-layer beams), mechanical response converges asymptotically to that of perfectly bonded beams.

In three-layer beams with asymmetric interfacial stiffnesses, stresses and displacement jumps redistribute toward the more compliant interface, while interfacial shear tractions concentrate at the stiffer interface.

future_work: Extending the single-variable formulation to layered systems possessing elastic mismatch between adjacent layers.
Implementing the single-variable model into numerical isogeometric collocation schemes.
Incorporating modeling of thick interlayers or transition zones between adjacent layers as weak layers.
Accounting for thermal loads, residual stresses, and misfit strains.
independent_variables: Longitudinal coordinate x2 and through-thickness coordinate x3
Nondimensional interfacial tangential stiffness parameters (K_S*h/ET, K1_S*h/ET, K2_S*h/ET)
Number of layers and stacking sequence (two-layer 0/0 and three-layer 0/0/0)
Transverse mechanical loading distribution (sinusoidal versus uniform load)
limitations_inferred: The formulation was benchmarked only against simply supported boundary conditions; other boundary configurations (e.g., clamped or free ends) were not evaluated.
The study is entirely analytical and benchmarked against 2D elasticity exact solutions; no physical experiments on actual physical specimens were conducted.
Analyses were confined to static mechanical loading; dynamic, vibratory, and time-dependent degradation behaviors were not addressed.
The model is strictly a one-dimensional beam formulation under plane strain and was not demonstrated on two-dimensional plates or three-dimensional continuum geometries.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The formulation is restricted to beams with layers made of the same homogeneous material, excluding the effect of elastic mismatch between layers.
Interfaces are treated as sharp zero-thickness surfaces with zero relative transverse displacement, neglecting physical transition zones or finite-thickness interlayers.
Assumptions are limited to small displacements, rotations, and strains.
Transverse normal stresses are neglected in formulating beam kinematics and equilibrium (sigma_33 = 0).
Residual manufacturing stresses and thermal gradient stresses are not incorporated in the presented beam equations.
The approximate zigzag kinematics assume piecewise linear longitudinal displacement through the thickness, unable to match the nonlinear intra-layer displacement profile of 2D elasticity.
main_results: The coupled system of three differential equations for layered beams with imperfect interfaces was decoupled into a single sixth-order differential equation in a fictitious bending displacement variable.

Closed-form analytical solutions for simply supported two- and three-layer beams under uniform and sinusoidal transverse loads demonstrated strong agreement with Pagano's 2D exact elasticity solutions.
Interfacial compliance significantly amplified local displacements and bending stresses while creating distinct interfacial displacement jumps.
Increasing interfacial stiffness caused the structural response to transition smoothly toward the perfectly bonded limit, nearly overlapping at K_S*h/ET = 10 for two layers and 5 for three layers.

Interfacial stiffness asymmetry in three-layer systems led to significant redistribution of stresses and displacements, shifting jumps to the compliant interface and tractions to the stiffer interface.
The transverse loading pattern (sinusoidal vs. uniform) played a secondary role compared to the interfacial compliance in determining local stress and displacement profiles.
modeling_methods: Single-variable zigzag beam theory.
Global first-order shear deformation kinematics enriched with local piecewise functions for interfacial displacement jumps.
Principle of Virtual Work for deriving homogenized equilibrium equations.
Decomposition of transverse displacement into bending and shear components to select a fictitious bending primal variable.
Sixth-order ordinary differential equation governing the fictitious bending displacement.
A posteriori evaluation of transverse shear and normal stresses through 2D local Cauchy equilibrium equations.
Comparison and validation against Pagano's 2D elasticity exact solutions via the transfer matrix method.
performance_metrics: Nondimensional through-thickness local longitudinal displacement (k)v2.
Nondimensional local bending normal stress (k)sigma22.
Nondimensional local transverse shear stress (k)sigma23 determined from local equilibrium.
Degree of correlation/overlap with 2D exact elasticity solutions.
possible_gap_implications: The single-variable zigzag formulation for sliding interfaces could provide a computationally efficient, shear-locking-free framework for modeling variable-stiffness structures (e.g., layer-jamming mechanisms or friction-controlled laminated continuum structures) without increasing degrees of freedom as layer count increases.

The present model's restriction to identical layer materials, zero-thickness interfaces without transverse separation, and small-strain linear kinematics requires extension before it can model soft robotic systems involving large deflections, compliant elastomer matrices, or hyperelastic materials.
paper.research_objective: To develop and verify an accurate and efficient single-variable zigzag formulation for beams composed of homogeneous layers of identical material with imperfect, sliding-compliant interfaces subjected to transverse mechanical loading.
paper.research_problem: Layered structures with imperfect, compliant bonds or delaminations exhibit complex local stress and displacement distributions that govern stiffness degradation and failure; standard multi-variable and discrete-layer structural theories are computationally demanding or prone to numerical issues such as shear locking in finite element implementations.
stiffness_mechanism: sliding between layers at imperfect interfaces

constitutive_assumptions: Interface stick-slip tangential behavior is represented by the Iwan model framework comprising parallel spring-slider (Jenkins) elements and a parallel linear spring accounting for residual stiffness.
Local friction obeys Coulomb's friction law with a constant friction coefficient relating slider critical slip force to normal contact force.
Rough surface contact material is modeled as elastic-perfectly plastic in finite element simulations.
Normal contact between two nominally flat rough surfaces is modeled equivalently as contact between a rough surface and a smooth rigid flat surface with combined roughness.
Normal contact interface interaction is modeled as hard contact, with frictionless tangential behavior during the normal loading stage in FEM.
Surface topography exhibits self-affine fractal properties generated via a modified two-variable Weierstrass-Mandelbrot (WM) function, neglecting surface waviness and form components.
Contact pressure distribution of contacting asperities is described by a twofold Weibull mixture probability density function.
Masing's hypothesis applies to reloading and unloading paths during cyclic tangential loading to form closed hysteresis loops.
The spatial distribution of contact pressure on the bolted joint interface is assumed to be uniform for simplicity.

constitutive_assumptions: Rough surface contact is equivalent to contact between a rigid flat plane and a rough surface.
Single asperity contact profile is simplified using a two-dimensional cosine profile according to the Majumdar-Bhushan (MB) model.
Deformation of individual asperities follows the Chang-Etsion-Bogy (CEB) model with discrete fully elastic and fully plastic regimes, neglecting intermediate elastoplastic transition states.
There is no mutual mechanical interaction among individual micro-asperities across the contact surface.
Normal contact forces distributed among individual micro-asperities (Jenkins units) follow a geometric series distribution.
All individual discrete Jenkins units possess identical tangential spring stiffness.
At any given scale, the number distribution of asperities is assumed uniform across different contact areas.
Surface topography and fractal parameters remain unchanged during sliding and cyclic tangential loading.
Unloading and reloading tangential force-displacement relationships follow Masing's mapping rule.
control_variables: Material properties of the contact pair (No. 45 steel: elastic modulus E = 209 GPa, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.27, hardness H = 157 MPa)
Number of Jenkins elements in the discrete Iwan model (empirically determined from total normal force and maximum contact force)
Minimum asperity length scale (set by measurement instrument resolution)
Nominal contact area
Tangential residual stiffness after macro-slip
dependent_variables: Real contact area and contact area ratio (Ar, A/Ar)
Normal contact stiffness and dimensionless normal stiffness (Ke, Kp, K*)
Total normal force (Fn) and maximum contact spot area (aL)
Tangential force (Fτ) and tangential shear stress (τ)
Initial tangential contact stiffness
Critical macro-slip displacement threshold (xslip)
Tangential hysteresis loop shape and energy dissipation area

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Classical MB-based contact models assume complete deformation for all asperities with a constant global critical contact area, causing calculation deviations for small contact areas and failing to capture the elastic-to-plastic temporal evolution of individual asperities.
Introducing asperity length scale and contact area as two independent variables yields a scale-dependent critical area expression and a continuous-scale asperity number distribution function.
Normal contact stiffness increases with normal load and fractal dimension D, but decreases with increasing fractal roughness G, exhibiting a local peak across roughness ranges.
Tangential stick-slip response exhibits tangential stiffness softening in the micro-slip regime followed by constant residual stiffness during macroscopic sliding.
Increasing normal load and friction coefficient shifts the macroscopic sliding onset to larger tangential displacements and linearly increases the macro-slip tangential force.
The improved fractal-discrete Iwan model demonstrates agreement with literature experimental hysteresis loops for steel specimens under normal loads between 200 N and 600 N.

experimental_setup: Validation was conducted against benchmark experimental data from secondary literature (Zong et al., 2022).
Specimens were sliding blocks of No. 45 steel with elastic modulus of 209 GPa, Poisson's ratio of 0.27, and hardness of 157 MPa.
Three rough surface slider profiles were evaluated: Slider 1 (D = 1.54, G = 3.99e-9 m), Slider 2 (D = 1.47, G = 4.44e-8 m), and Slider 3 (D = 1.43, G = 4.71e-8 m).
Normal loads were applied in the range of 200 N to 600 N (specifically around 203 N–208 N, 404 N–406 N, and 606 N–608 N).
Cyclic tangential displacement loading was applied with amplitudes between 60 μm and 100 μm.
future_work: Replacing the constant macroscopic friction coefficient with local, fractal-described friction coefficients for individual micro-contacts to enhance physical fidelity.
Developing theoretical or physics-based formulations for initial tangential stiffness to eliminate reliance on empirical parameter identification.
Applying the stick-slip contact formulation in structural finite element simulations of mechanical assembly interfaces.
independent_variables: Normal load / normal force (Fn)
Fractal dimension (D)
Fractal roughness parameter (G)
Tangential displacement and cyclic displacement amplitude (x, xmax)
Friction coefficient (μ)
limitations_inferred: The model was validated solely on metallic (No. 45 steel) contact interfaces from literature and was not demonstrated on soft, elastomeric, hyperelastic, or viscoelastic materials common in soft robotics.
The fractal contact formulation assumes two-dimensional profile representations extended isotropically, without accounting for surface texture anisotropy or directional lay.
Dynamic inertia, rate dependence, and frictional thermal effects during continuous high-frequency stick-slip cycles are not incorporated.
Loading is restricted to unidirectional tangential shear coupled with normal compression, omitting multi-axial bending or torsional interfacial loading.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Neighboring asperities on the contact interface are assumed to have no mutual interaction.
Wear and morphological evolution of the surface topography during sliding are not considered.
Initial tangential stiffness in the discrete Iwan formulation relies on experimental parameter identification rather than direct physical derivation, weakening physical interpretability.
A uniform macroscopic friction coefficient is assumed rather than localized micro-contact friction coefficients.
The single-asperity CEB formulation assumes an abrupt transition between fully elastic and fully plastic states, omitting intermediate elastoplastic phases.
main_results: The continuous-scale fractal model resolves the inconsistency of classical MB models regarding plastic deformation of small asperities by establishing that asperities deform elastically before plastic yield.

Dimensionless normal contact stiffness rises monotonically with normal load and fractal dimension D, but decreases with fractal roughness G, showing a distinct peak across certain roughness ranges that shifts toward higher roughness as D increases.
Normal stiffness derived from the CEB-based continuous-scale model exhibits a quadratic-like growth curve with normal force compared to the more linear progression seen in KE-based models.
Tangential hysteresis curves display two distinct stages: stiffness degradation during micro-slip and stable residual stiffness during macro-slip.
Higher normal loads and friction coefficients delay the onset of macro-slip to larger tangential displacements and scale the saturation sliding force linearly.
Simulated hysteresis loops from the coupled continuous-scale fractal and discrete Iwan model show close alignment with experimental data across different surface topographies and normal load levels.
modeling_methods: Continuous-scale fractal surface representation based on Morag-Etsion (ME) and Weierstrass-Mandelbrot (W-M) theories.
Chang-Etsion-Bogy (CEB) single-asperity contact model defining elastic-fully plastic transitions.
Two-variable continuous-scale asperity distribution function n'(a, l) dependent on asperity scale and contact spot area.
Discrete Iwan stick-slip model with parallel Jenkins elements and geometric-series normal load distribution.
Masing mapping rule for predicting cyclic tangential force-displacement hysteresis loops during unloading and reloading.
performance_metrics: Dimensionless normal contact stiffness (K*) versus dimensionless normal load (Fn*)
Relative area proportion of micro-contacts smaller than a specified area (A/Ar versus a/aL)
Tangential force-displacement hysteresis curve profile and enclosed loop area (frictional energy dissipation)
Initial tangential contact stiffness
Macroscopic sliding friction force
Critical macro-slip displacement threshold (xslip)
Correlation between theoretical hysteresis loops and experimental measurements
possible_gap_implications: The continuous-scale formulation mitigates scale-truncation errors for small contact interfaces in numerical structural assembly simulations, but adapting it to soft robotics would require reformulating asperity mechanics for large-deformation hyperelastic and viscoelastic polymers.
paper.research_objective: To establish an improved continuous-scale fractal and discrete Iwan stick-slip contact mechanics model by introducing asperity length scale and contact spot area as independent variables, deriving a scale-dependent critical area and asperity distribution function, and characterizing interfacial tangential hysteresis under combined normal and tangential loading.
paper.research_problem: Existing Majumdar-Bhushan (MB) based fractal-Iwan coupling models assume that all micro-asperities undergo complete deformation and share a globally constant elastoplastic critical area, leading to calculation deviations for normal forces on small contact spots and rendering the model incompatible with small nominal contact areas in structural assembly simulations.
